examples.label: CPTS Ch06 — monitor scan bandwidth impact
examples.command:
sudo apt install vnstat
sudo vnstat -l -i eth0
# Run before and during Nessus/OpenVAS scan to observe bandwidth usage

notes: vnstat tracks bandwidth per interface - run it during active scanning to prove you stayed within agreed rate limits (RoE) and to spot when a scan is hammering the target. Evidence/hygiene, not an attack. Use vnstat to observe network impact of vulnerability scans. Unauthenticated Nessus scans typically generate ~150-400 kbit/s; authenticated scans are lower. Monitor to avoid exceeding agreed-upon bandwidth limits in client engagements. Also covered in: CPTS Ch06 (Vulnerability Assessment).

recommended.note: Kick off the authenticated scan you're monitoring.

name: vnstat - Monitor Scan Bandwidth
description: Watch live interface throughput while scanning so an aggressive scan doesn't saturate the link or trip network monitoring.

defense.why_it_works: vnstat is a console network-traffic monitor that logs per-interface bandwidth over time. In an assessment it is used to gauge how much traffic a scan generates - an opsec / monitoring aid, not an attack against the target.
defense.prerequisites: Local access on the testing host with vnstat installed and watching the scanning interface.
defense.impact: Awareness of scan bandwidth and footprint, helping the tester stay under rate-based detection thresholds and avoid disrupting the target network.
defense.detection: None on the target - vnstat only reads local interface counters and sends nothing to the target.
defense.artifacts: No victim-side evidence; a local vnstat database on the tester's host.
defense.misconfiguration: Vulnerability scanning reveals services with unpatched CVEs, default configurations, or known-weak settings. The absence of a patch management process allows critical vulnerabilities to remain exploitable for months or years. Scan results that are not acted upon create a false sense of security.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# OpenVAS/Nessus finding typical vulnerable targets:
# CVSSv3: 9.8 - Apache Struts2 RCE (CVE-2017-5638) - unpatched
# CVSSv3: 8.8 - Tomcat manager with default creds (admin/admin)
# CVSSv3: 10.0 - MS17-010 (EternalBlue) - SMBv1 enabled, unpatched

# Unpatched = patch not applied within SLA:
# Critical (CVSS 9+): patch within 24-72 hours
# High (CVSS 7-8.9): patch within 7 days
# Medium: patch within 30 days
defense.secure_config:
# Establish a vulnerability management program:
# 1. Scan weekly with authenticated scans (Nessus/OpenVAS/Qualys)
# 2. Integrate scan results with ticketing (Jira/ServiceNow)
# 3. Set SLA by severity: Critical 72h, High 7d, Medium 30d
# 4. Verify patches with re-scan

# CVSS scoring -> risk-based prioritization:
# Not all CVSSv3 9+ are exploitable in your environment
# Use EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) to prioritize by actual exploitation likelihood

# Defense-in-depth: patch is the fix, but compensating controls while patching:
# WAF rule for web vuln CVEs
# Network segment to isolate vulnerable service
# IDS signature for exploit traffic
